Introduction

Overview of the Child Trust Fund

A Child Trust Fund (CTF) is a savings product that provides tax relief for children. It was designed to provide a sum of money when a child reached adulthood. The CTF scheme started on 6 April 2005 and a CTF (with a government contribution) was provided to all children born between 1 September 2002 and 3 January 2011. If an account was not opened by the child’s parent, one was opened on the child’s behalf by HMRC.

The scheme was closed to new entrants in January 2011, but existing accounts remain open for contributions and management purposes. Children who are not eligible for a CTF may be eligible for a Junior Individual Savings Account (JISA). A child cannot have both a CTF and a Junior ISA. A child with a CTF can have their CTF transferred into a Junior ISA.

Income and gains generated by CTF investments are exempt from Income Tax and Capital Gains Tax. The income generated from parental subscriptions to the CTF does not count toward the parent’s income under the settlements legislation (section 629 of the Income Tax (Trading and Other Income) Act 2005).

A CTF is an investment account managed in accordance with the CTF regulations under terms agreed between the CTF provider and the registered contact.

The provider holds investments on behalf of the child, and claims repayment of Income Tax deducted at source, by submitting tax claim forms to Charities, Savings & International 1 (read the section on contacting HMRC). Claims in respect of insurance products are made by the insurance company or friendly society providing insurance cover (who may be different to the provider).

Anybody can make subscriptions into a child’s CTF. Amounts can only be withdrawn from a CTF before the child’s 18th birthday to pay account management charges made by the CTF provider, or if the child is terminally ill. If the child dies before they reach 18, the investments in the CTF become part of the child’s estate.

The guidance notes and legislation

The guidance notes are for providers and explain how to operate the CTF scheme.

Providers are reminded of their obligations to comply with the Financial Conduct Authority Handbook (FCA) of rules and guidance on the Financial Conduct Authority website, and anti-money laundering legislation.

The main legislation is in the Child Trust Funds Act 2004.

The detailed rules are contained in the Child Trust Funds Regulations 2004 No.1450, and all subsequent amendment regulations and the Child Trust Funds (Insurance Companies) Regulations 2004 No.2680.

CTF definitions

51% subsidiary

Fifty one per cent subsidiary has the meaning given by Chapter 3 of part 24 of the Corporation Tax Act 2010.

75% subsidiary

Seventy five per cent subsidiary has the meaning given by Chapter 3 of part 24 of the Corporation Tax Act 2010.

Adoption order

Has the meaning in section 46(1) of the Adoption and Children Act 2002(1) or section 28 of the Adoption and Children (Scotland) Act 2007 or of Adoption Order in Article 2(2) of the Adoption (Northern Ireland) Order 1987, as the case may be, and includes any corresponding order under the Adoption (Scotland) Act 1978, and any order of a court in the Isle of Man or any of the Channel Islands which, under section 108 of the Adoption and Children Act 2002, is declared to correspond to an adoption order made under that act.

Alternative finance arrangements

Arrangements falling within section 47 or 49 of the Finance Act 2005.

Assurance undertaking

Has the meaning in Article 2 of the Council Directive of 5 November 2002 concerning life assurance (No. 2002/83).

Bank of England base rate

The rate announced from time to time by the Monetary Policy Committee of the Bank of England as the official dealing rate, being the rate at which the bank is willing to enter into transactions for providing short-term liquidity in the money markets.

Board of HMRC

The Board of HMRC is chaired by the lead non-executive and includes the permanent secretaries, the non-executive board members and the chief finance officer.

Building society

A building society within the meaning of the Building Societies Act 1986, or the Irish Building Societies Act 1989.

Collective Investment Schemes Sourcebook (COLL)

This is the sourcebook issued by the FCA under section 243 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000.

Company

A company is any body corporate having a share capital other than:

an open-ended investment company within the meaning of section 236 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000

a UK Undertakings for Collective Investment Transferable Securities (UCITS)

Credit union

A society registered as a credit union under the Industrial Provident Societies Act 1965 or the Credit Unions (Northern Ireland) Order 1985.

EEA State

Find a list of states of the EEA on the GOV.UK website.

Equities

Shares in a company incorporated anywhere in the world and officially listed or admitted to trading on a recognised stock exchange.

European Institution an EEA firm of the kind mentioned in paragraph 5(a) to (d), (f) and (h) of schedule 3 to Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 which is an authorised person for the purposes of that act as a result of qualifying for authorisation under paragraph 12(1) to (4) and (7) of that schedule.

FCA

The Financial Conduct Authority.

Gilt edged security

Securities which are gilt edged securities are listed in paragraphs 1 and 1A of schedule 9 of the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992.

Guardian

A guardian of a child within the meaning in section 5 of the Children Act 1989, section 7 of the Children (Scotland) Act 1995 or Article 2(2) of the Children (Northern Ireland) Order 1995, as the case may be.

Incorporated friendly society

A society incorporated under the Friendly Societies Act 1992.

Insolvency event

The procedures listed in the definition of ‘insolvency event’ in regulation 19(15) of the Payment Services Regulations 2009.

Insurance company

a person (other than a friendly society) who has permission under part 4 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 to effect or carry out contracts of insurance

an EEA firm of the kind mentioned in section 5(d) of Schedule 3 to the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 which carries on:

business which consists of the effecting or carrying out contracts of insurance

business through a branch or agency in the UK

Insurer

a person who has permission under part 4 of Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 to effect or carry out contracts of insurance

an EEA firm of the kind mentioned in section 5(d) of schedule 3 to Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 which has permission under section 15 of that schedule (as a result of qualifying for authorisation under section 12 of that schedule) to effect or carry out contracts of insurance

Investment trust

An investment trust has the same meaning as in section 1158 of the Corporation Tax Act 2010.

Matured CTF account

An account which is to be treated as a continuing account of the account holder who held the CTF before their 18th birthday, who has not given instructions to their provider.

Non-UCITS retail scheme

A non-UCITS retail scheme is a scheme that satisfies the relevant requirements of COLL and includes a ‘recognised scheme’ by virtue of section 270 or 272 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, which would fall within the requirements of COLL if it were an authorised fund.

Parental responsibility

Under general law parents who are married to each other will each have parental responsibility. Where parents are not married the mother will automatically have parental responsibility, as will the father if:

the father is registered on the birth certificate

parents agree by means of a parental responsibility agreement

a court so orders

Other individuals who will have parental responsibility include:

adoptive parents

a step-parent under a parental responsibility agreement

testamentary or special guardians

a person a child is living with under a residence order

Protected account

An account which is a matured CTF account or an ISA holding cash or investments transferred by the account provider when no instructions have been given by the account holder on their 18th birthday.

Recognised stock exchange

‘Recognised stock exchange’ means:

any market of a recognised investment exchange which is for the time being designated as a recognised stock exchange for the purposes of section 1005 of the Income Tax Act 2007 by an order made by the Commissioners for HMRC

any market outside the United Kingdom which for the time being so designated

It includes the London Stock Exchange, the PLUS-listed market, and any such stock exchange outside the UK as is designated in an Order of HMRC.

To find out more, read a list of stock exchanges that have been designated as recognised stock exchanges.

The phrase ‘listed on a recognised stock exchange’ in respect of shares and securities is now defined at section 1005(4) of the Income Tax Act 2007. It means shares and securities which are admitted to trading on that exchange and included in the official UK list maintained by the Financial Services Authority as the UK Listing Authority or are officially listed in a qualifying country outside the UK in accordance with provisions corresponding to those generally applicable in EEA states.

Recognised UCITS

An undertaking established in the UK or an EEA State within the meaning given by section 236A and 271A of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, and which is a recognised scheme for the purposes of part 17 of that act.

This includes an undertaking established in Gibraltar which is a UCITS under the law of Gibraltar which implemented Directive 2009/65/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 July 2009 on the co-ordination of laws, regulations and administrative provisions relating to undertakings for collective investment in transferable securities.

The EEA consists of the 27 member states of the EU, plus Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway. A list of states of the EU is available.

Registered contact

The responsible person who may give instructions to the provider with respect to the management of the CTF, or The Share Foundation.

Registered friendly society

A society within the meaning of the Friendly Societies Act 1992 and includes a society treated as a registered friendly society by virtue of section 96(2) of that Act.

Relevant authorised person

A firm mentioned in section 697(2)(b) of the Income Tax (Trading and Other Income) Act 2005.

Relevant collective investment scheme

An authorised unit trust, an authorised open-ended investment company, or a recognised scheme, as defined in section 237(3) of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000.

Responsible person

A person (not a local authority) who is aged 16 or over and who has parental responsibility for the child for whom the CTF is opened.

Security

A security means any loan stock or similar security of a company whether secured or unsecured. Qualifying securities may therefore include loans, loan stocks (whether secured or not) debentures, and Eurobonds, either in registered or bearer form.

Special guardian

Has the meaning in section 14A of the Children Act 1989.

Stakeholder CTF

In brief, the investments held in a stakeholder CTF must be selected according to the age of the child, the CTF must accept single subscriptions of £10 or more, and the maximum management charge that can be levied is 1.5%. In the context of CTF a ‘stakeholder product’ is separate to the definition provided by Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, the charge does not need to reduce to 1% after 10 years.

Strip

Strips involve the separation of the interest ‘coupons’ from the underlying principal on which the interest is payable.

Subscription year

The first subscription year starts the day the CTF is opened and ends on the day before the child’s next birthday. The succeeding years start on the child’s birthday and end on the day before the next birthday. In any year where the CTF closes (due to death of the child, or the child’s 18th birthday) the year of subscription ends when the CTF closes.

UK UCITS

a) a collective investment scheme authorised under section 31(1)(a) of Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, which complies with the requirements to be a ‘UCITS scheme’ for the purposes of the Collective Investment Schemes Sourcebook (see in particular COLL 1.2.2).

b) a part of a UK UCITS mentioned in paragraph (a) of this definition which would be a sub-fund of an umbrella scheme which is a UK UCITS.

Units in, or shares of, a UK UCITS or recognised UCITS

The rights (however described) of the holders of the units or shares in that UK UCITS or recognised UCITS.

With-profits fund

A fund maintained by an insurer in respect of a particular part of its long-term business for which:

separate accounting records are maintained by the insurer in respect of all income and expenditure relating to that part of its business

the benefits payable in respect of policies allocated to that fund are determined partly by reference to a discretion exercisable by any person

The CTF provider

Who can provide CTFs

Only providers approved by the Board of HMRC can be CTF providers.

A CTF provider must be:

an authorised person within the meaning of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 who has permission (other than an interim permission) to carry on one or more of the activities specified in articles 14, 21, 25, 37, 40, 45, 51ZA, 51ZC, 51ZE, 53 and, insofar as it applies to any of those activities, Article 64, of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001

a European institution with a UK base which carries on one or more of the activities as specified in the articles

a building society

a person falling within section 991 of the Income Tax Act 2007 (including a credit union)

an insurance company

an incorporated friendly society

a credit union which is an authorised person within the meaning of section 31(1)(a) of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 who has permission to carry on one or more of the activities specified in article 5 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001

a registered friendly society

any other assurance undertaking

Providers must not be prevented from acting as a CTF provider by any limitations or requirements imposed under part 4A of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, or by any prohibition or prohibition order in or made under that act.

Before they can be approved by the Board, anyone wishing to become a provider of CTFs must:

where the person agrees to accept Revenue allocated accounts, to allow instructions from the registered contact for management of the CTF to be made by post (whether or not other methods are used)

agree to publicise (and update where appropriate) statements of the minimum amount which may be subscribed to the CTF on a single occasion and the permitted means of payment of subscriptions

agree to publicise (and update where appropriate) statements of the extent to which social, environmental or ethical decision are taken into account in selecting, retaining or realising investments

agree to tell anyone who wants to make subscriptions to a CTF (other than the child) that the subscription is a gift to the child

make sure that a child’s unique reference number will only be used for the purposes of that child’s CTF and of fulfilling the requirements of the CTF regulations with regard to that CTF

make sure that the amount of the initial or special contribution to a CTF (whether there is a supplementary contribution to the CTF, and whether the CTF is a Revenue allocated account) is information held for the purpose of the child’s CTF (and of fulfilling the requirements of the CTF regulations with regard to the CTF) only, and shall not be used for other purposes (including marketing other products)

The provider must also give details of the bank account CTF government contributions must be paid into.

Tax representatives

An approved provider who has an assurance undertaking will have to either appoint a tax representative, make arrangements with the board for some other person to make sure that their duties as a provider are met, or make other arrangements with the board to make sure that their duties are met.

A tax representative must be:

an individual who is resident in the UK or a company that has a business establishment in the UK

entitled to act on behalf of the provider in relation to the duties set out in the regulations

responsible for ensuring that the provider meets the duties set out in the regulations

personally liable where the provider fails to meet these duties

A tax representative’s appointment is treated as being terminated where the board has reason to believe that the tax representative has failed to make sure that the provider met their prescribed duties, or does not have adequate resources to make sure that the duties are met.

The board will notify the provider of the termination and the date when it takes effect.

Accepting Revenue allocated accounts

A provider can agree to accept Revenue allocated accounts (read the section on ‘Revenue allocated accounts’) at the time of application for approval. The Revenue allocated accounts must be stakeholder accounts. Where a provider wishes to accept Revenue allocated accounts after application they can do so by applying in writing to HMRC.

A provider cannot agree to accept Revenue allocated accounts unless they are able to offer the account themselves. They cannot accept Revenue allocated accounts which are then set up with another provider.

A provider can only stop accepting Revenue allocated accounts by writing to HMRC, giving 30 calendar days’ notice of their intention to stop. The provider must continue to manage any existing CTFs that were opened as Revenue allocated accounts.

Stopping being a provider

A person will stop being a provider if:

HMRC withdraws approval

the provider voluntarily stops

they can no longer qualify as a provider

Formal withdrawal of approval

HMRC may withdraw approval from a provider if:

it has reason to believe that the provider is failing

the provider has failed to manage their CTFs in accordance with the regulations

the provider is not qualified to act as a provider

HMRC will issue a notice of withdrawal of approval, which will specify the:

disqualifying circumstances

that the withdrawal is only effective from the date on which the last of the accounts has been transferred

that from the date of the notice, the provider must not accept subscriptions or open new accounts

The notice will explain how to make an appeal against the withdrawal. Providers may appeal within 30 calendar days of the date the notice is issued.

If no appeal is made against the notice of withdrawal of approval or an appeal against withdrawal has not been successful, the provider must write to each registered contact, or to the child where there is no registered contact, or to The Share Foundation within 30 calendar days of the date they stopped to qualify. The written notice must tell the registered contact, child, or the Share Foundation that they have the right to transfer the CTF to another provider.

A CTF provider will not cease to act as an account provider until all accounts have been transferred to another provider. The Provider will be unable to accept any new accounts or subscriptions during this time.

Voluntarily stopping being a provider

A provider who intends to stop managing CTFs must give notice in writing to HMRC and to each registered contact (or the child if there is no registered contact for the CTF, or The Share Foundation) at least 30 calendar days before the date they intend to stop. HMRC can then check that the provider has fulfilled all their obligations under the regulations. The notice to the registered contact, child or The Share Foundation must tell them they have a right to transfer the CTF to another provider.

A CTF provider will not cease to act as an account provider until all accounts have been transferred to another provider. The Provider will be unable to accept any new accounts or subscriptions during this time.

Why you may no longer qualify as a provider

A person no longer qualifies as a provider when they are no longer eligible, or when:

there is an insolvency event in relation to the account provider

a debt relief order is made (under part 7A of the Insolvency Act 1986)

an application has been made for a bank insolvency order or a bank administration order

a relevant authorised person or an assurance undertaking, is subject of the equivalent of an insolvency event, a debt relief order or has had a receiver appointed to manage its property

in the case of a European institution, you do not have a UK base to carry out your activities

in the case of a building society, a person falling within section 991 of the Income Tax Act 2007 or a Credit Union

it stops being a building society or to be a person falling within section 991 Income Tax Act 2007 or a Credit Union, as the case may be

its directors have made a proposal under part 1 of the Insolvency Act 1986 for a composition in satisfaction of its debts or a scheme of arrangement of its affairs

a receiver or manager of its property has been appointed

A provider who no longer qualifies must give notice in writing to HMRC and to each registered contact (or to the child where there is no registered contact, or to The Share Foundation) within 30 calendar days of the date they stopped to qualify. This notice must tell the registered contact or child that they have the right to transfer the CTF to another provider.

A CTF provider will not cease to act as an account provider until all accounts have been transferred to another provider. The Provider will be unable to accept any new accounts or subscriptions during this time.

Returns required when you stop being a provider

A provider who has stopped managing CTFs must submit an annual claim form (if they have made any interim claims), and a return of information to the date when they stopped.

If you have been forced to stop, or approval has been withdrawn, the person appointed to end the CTF scheme should perform these duties.

Delegation of the provider’s functions or responsibilities

Under the management agreement entered into with the registered contact, a provider can delegate any of the functions or responsibility of the management of the CTF to another person. That person does not need to be an approved CTF provider. The provider remains responsible for the actions of the person they have delegated any CTF function or responsibility to.

Types of Child Trust Fund

Stakeholder and non-stakeholder

There are 2 types of CTF: a stakeholder CTF or a non-stakeholder CTF. It cannot be a mix of the 2. A change from one type to the other can be made by an internal transfer, or on external transfer to another provider.

Both stakeholder and non-stakeholder CTF accounts mature on the account holder’s 18th birthday. If no instructions are given to a CTF provider, the account becomes a matured CTF account.

The stakeholder conditions on the CTF account do not apply to a matured CTF account. The investment profile should remain unchanged and the term and conditions should remain substantially the same as before the account holder’s 18th birthday.

Stakeholder conditions

A stakeholder CTF is a stocks and shares account characterised by additional rules to protect account holders. The stakeholder CTF has 6 conditions, all of which must be satisfied. The conditions cover:

the types of investments allowed

exposure to equities

diversification and suitability

means of payment of subscriptions

the minimum subscription

charge capping

The terms stakeholder or non-stakeholder refer to the overall profile of the account, rather than the underlying investments in the account. Both types of accounts can hold a variety of qualifying investments (read the section on ‘Qualifying investments for the CTF’). However, the stakeholder account has a more restricted set of qualifying investments.

The stakeholder conditions apply to the entire stakeholder account. That is, the provider must make sure the overall account has an exposure to equities and is well diversified. With effect from 6 April 2017 lifestyling is no longer a requirement. The required means of payment, minimum subscription and charge cap apply to the overall stakeholder account, which encompasses all investments held within the account.

Investments in a stakeholder CTF

A variety of investments may be held in the stakeholder CTF, however a stakeholder CTF cannot hold directly the following investments:

shares in an investment trust

securities of an investment trust

with-profits endowments or insurance policies

units or shares in dual-priced collective investment schemes

rights in dual-priced contracts of insurance

shares in companies

securities in companies unless the value of the securities is guaranteed not to fall below 80% of the original price paid

cash in deposit accounts or share accounts with building societies where the interest rate is more than 1% below the Bank of England base rate

depositary interests representing any of the previous investments

Full details of the restrictions on the type of investments not allowed within the stakeholder CTF can be found in the ‘Restrictions on qualifying investments in a stakeholder CTF’ section.

However, the investments excluded may be held indirectly in the stakeholder CTF — for example, where a single-priced collective investment scheme invests in shares of an investment trust, this is permissible.

Exposure to equities

The units, shares or rights held in a stakeholder CTF must have an exposure to equities. No minimum level of exposure to equities has been specified, giving providers the flexibility to modify the level to take account of market conditions.

Diversification and suitability

The provider must have regard to the need for diversification of investments in the stakeholder CTF, whilst bearing in mind the circumstances of the account.

In practice, diversification would require a spread of investments across a range of different markets, sectors and securities. The following types of investment strategy would not be regarded as suitable for a stakeholder CTF:

a high proportion of high-risk bonds, whether long-dated or sub-investment grade

high exposure to high-risk equities

investment in derivatives (except for efficient portfolio management)

a high level of currency risk

high exposure to highly-geared firms or funds

Funds that are index trackers would meet these diversification requirements, as long as the index itself is adequately diversified. For example, a tracker fund for the FTSE All Share or FTSE-100 would meet the diversification requirement. Any other tracker that invested in a balanced portfolio of UK and overseas shares, fixed-interest securities, index linked stock and cash deposits would also be suitable.

The provider must also have regard to the purposes of the CTF in considering the suitability of investments, or any investment strategy or option proposed. This puts a general duty of care on the provider.

CTF subscriptions

Providers must accept subscriptions to the stakeholder CTF by cheque, Direct Debit, standing order, and direct credit. They are not required to accept other forms of payment, such as cash, credit card, debit card or any combination of these, but can if they so wish. There are no restrictions or requirements on payment methods for non-stakeholder CTFs.

Providers must accept a minimum one-off subscription of £10 to the stakeholder CTF (provided that the payment is an acceptable form of payment to the provider, which will include the required means of payments described in means of payment of subscriptions in the previous paragraph.

Providers can offer to accept smaller amounts if they wish.

Charge capping

Providers can make charges for management and other expenses but they are capped. This means that a CTF provider’s management charges cannot not exceed 1.5% per annum of the value of a CTF stakeholder investment account that they have managed for a whole year.

The value of each stakeholder CTF is the sum of the value of the investments (including cash) held in the CTF, for example, the number of units multiplied by unit value. Costs included in the charge cap are:

all distributing and marketing costs, including:

product development

advertising and promotion

acquisition

capturing client data

completion

submitting applications

new business processing, including:

processing applications

compliance activity

issuing contract documentation

ongoing administration, including:

collecting and investing contributions

contract accounting

investment management (excluding taxation and dealing costs)

account servicing (statements, updates, quotes and so on)

claims administration, including:

processing instructions

realisation of funds (excluding any costs associated with selling assets)

payment

updating records

fund management (excluding taxation or dealing costs)

custodian charges

legal and audit costs

Where the investments in the CTF are directly or indirectly held in a collective investment or life insurance vehicle, any management or administration fees charged in respect of investments held by the collective investment or life insurance vehicle must be included in the charge cap calculation if they fall into any of the categories in the costs included in the cap charge section.

Certain expenses and charges can be deducted from a CTF before the investments in the CTF are valued and the charge cap calculated. These are:

Stamp Duty, Stamp Duty Reserve Tax and dealing charges (including either direct or indirect, and any dilution levy) associated with the sale and purchase of investments in the CTF, (since 6 April 2017 lifestyling is no longer a requirement)

any expenses incurred in complying with an order of the court or other legal requirements which could include costs associated with:

HMRC refunds

criminal including fraudulent action

suspension and forfeiture costs

divorce costs

recovery of excessive costs of bankruptcy

recovery of the proceeds of crime

all forms of taxation

charges for provision of an annual report or accounts, where the registered contact has chosen to receive a copy of the report and accounts for any concern whose shares and units are held in the CTF

associated charges where the registered contact has chosen to attend meetings of investors for any concern whose shares and units are held in the CTF, to vote, or to receive any other investor information

Any costs of an internal or external transfer of a CTF must be met from within the charge cap — no separate charge can be made to any individual CTF.

The provider must value each stakeholder CTF daily, weekly or monthly, and they must explain which method they will use to the registered contact in writing. The provider cannot change the method within 12 months of the last written notification.

Where the valuation is carried out weekly or monthly, the same specified day in the week or month must be used (or the day after if that day is not a working day). Also, the value on the day of valuation is assumed to be the value for each day, until the next time of valuation.

CTF applications

CTF terms and conditions

A CTF is a scheme of investment managed in accordance with the CTF regulations by the provider under terms agreed between the provider and the registered contact. The CTF must be held in the name of the child.

All children eligible for a CTF account should have one. HMRC no longer issues vouchers or replacement vouchers. Where, exceptionally, CTF entitlement is established after 1 January 2013 HMRC will contact providers on a case-by-case basis to arrange for a CTF to be opened.

Providers’ CTF terms and conditions must specify in writing that:

1. The CTF investments shall be in the beneficial ownership of the child.

2. Except for cash deposits, National Savings products and certain insurance policies, the title to the CTF investments will be registered in either:

the name of the provider

the name of the provider’s nominee

3. Where a share certificate or other document evidencing title to a CTF investment is issued, it will be held by the provider or as the provider may direct.

4. Where insurance policies are with an insurer who is also a provider, the title to the policies shall be vested in the registered contact, and the policy document or other document showing title to the insurance policy shall be held by the registered contact.

5. If the registered contact chooses, the provider will arrange for them to receive a copy of the annual report and accounts issued by every company or other concern in respect of shares, securities or units which are held directly in the CTF (a separate charge may be levied for this service).

6. If the registered contact chooses, the provider will arrange for them to:

attend shareholders’, securities holders’ or unit holders’ meetings

vote and receive, in addition to the annual report and accounts, any other information issued to shareholders, securities holders or unit holders (a separate charge may be levied for these services)

7. The provider will make sure that any person he delegates any of their functions or responsibilities to under the terms agreed with the registered contact is competent to carry them out.

8. On the instructions of the registered contact and within the time stipulated by them, the CTF with all rights and obligations shall be transferred free of charge (except charges such as Stamp Duty and other dealing costs connected with disposal or acquisition of investments) to another provider.

9. Where an account is transferred to the provider it will be accepted free of charge (except charges such as Stamp Duty and other dealing costs associated with disposal or acquisition of investments).

10. Where the provider offers both types of CTF on the instructions of the registered contact and within the time stipulated by them, the CTF shall become a CTF of the other description (any necessary changes in the investments being made) free of expense (except expenses such as Stamp Duty and other dealing costs connected with disposal or acquisition of investments).

11. The provider may place a minimum period on the time for transfer stipulated by the registered contact (this period must not exceed 30 days, and should represent a reasonable period required for practical implementation of the transfer).

12. The provider must notify the registered contact if, because of any failure to satisfy the provisions of the CTF regulations, a CTF has, or will, become void.

Imaging vouchers, application forms and written declarations

The CTF voucher contained the child’s name and date of birth, their unique reference number, the amount of the government contribution and the voucher’s expiry date. The value of CTF vouchers differed according to the personal circumstance of the child.

HMRC no longer issues CTF vouchers.

CTF vouchers, declarations and application forms, transfer forms and registered contact applications can be scanned and stored in a digital form (black and white or in colour), and then the paper originals can be destroyed.

The digital images will be regarded as applications for the purposes of the CTF rules if:

the image of the documents (and any hard copy printouts) are readable

the provider can provide a hard copy of the imaged documents to HMRC within a reasonable time when requested

Since 6 April 2009 providers could open a CTF without seeing a voucher.

Since 1 January 2013, when a child’s entitlement to a CTF was established, HMRC has contacted providers on a case-by-case basis to arrange for a CTF to be opened.

Revenue allocated accounts

Where a voucher was issued, and a CTF was not opened within 7 days of the expiry date on the voucher, a provider who had agreed to accept Revenue allocated accounts was instructed to open a stakeholder CTF for the child. All Revenue allocated accounts must be stakeholder accounts.

When the provider confirmed that the CTF had been opened, HMRC issued a letter to the person who claimed Child Benefit for the child, informing them that the CTF had been opened, and providing details of the provider with whom the CTF is held.

In a small number of cases where a child was taken into care by a local authority soon after birth and before a Child Benefit claim was made, HMRC instructed providers to open a CTF for the child.

In a few cases the child’s parent made it clear that they did not want to be contacted by providers. In these cases HMRC gave the name of the correspondent as Mrs CTF Liaison Officer, with the address of the CTFO office in Washington. Following the closure of the CTF office, providers should mark those records to prevent future correspondence being issued (until a valid application to take on the registered contact role is received).

The registered contact

The registered contact

There can only be one registered contact at any time. The registered contact is the only person who can give instructions to the provider on management of the investments in the CTF.

The registered contact must be a person aged 16 or older. If the child is 16 or older, the child may choose to be the registered contact. If the child is under 16 only a person who has parental responsibility for the child can be the registered contact.

A person with parental responsibility can only be the registered contact until their role ends when the account holder becomes 18. Only the account holder can give instructions to their CTF provider when they reach 16 and take over the registered contact role, or when their account matures at 18.

A registered contact does not stop when the child is 16, but at this point the child has the right to take over the registered contact role. They can do this without the agreement of the existing registered contact.

The Share Foundation has been appointed to act as the registered contact for children who are looked after by local authorities. Children in local authority care can take over the registered contact role when they become 16. The Share Foundation stops being the registered contact when a child reaches 18.

Applying to be the registered contact

Where there is no registered contact, a person who satisfies the registered contact conditions can apply to become the registered contact.

Written application to be the registered contact

The application must contain:

the applicant’s title (if any) first name, surname, and middle initials

the applicant’s address, including postcode

the child’s title (if any), first name, surname, and middle initials

the child’s address, including postcode

the child’s date of birth

the child’s unique reference number

Providers can use the wording in the specimen form.

Applicants must make a declaration that the information given in the application is correct. The following declaration will satisfy the requirements of the regulations:

“I declare that:

I am 16 years of age or over

I am the child or I have parental responsibility for the child (delete the words that do not apply)

I will be the registered contact for the CTF

(where the application is not in writing) I authorise the CTF provider to record the terms of this declaration in a written declaration made on my behalf”

Declarations must also contain an agreement by the applicant to the CTF terms and conditions, and the applicant’s signature.

Applications must include certain authorities. The following authorities will satisfy the requirements of the regulations:

“I authorise [provider’s name] to hold the child’s HMRC contributions, subscriptions, CTF investments, interest, dividends and any other rights or proceeds in respect of those investments and cash, and to make on the child’s behalf any claims to relief from tax in respect of CTF investments.”

This authority continues until it is replaced following a change in registered contact, or transfer to another provider. If the existing registered contact stops being the registered contact, the previously-given authority continues until it is replaced.

Where The Share Foundation becomes the registered contact they are deemed to have agreed the existing terms and conditions of the CTF. They should not be asked to complete an application form but they are required to make the declaration and authorisation required by the regulations.

You can download the application form (ODT, 8.63KB) to be a registered contact.

Non-written application to be the registered contact

Where an application and declaration is made other than in writing (for example, by telephone, email or fax), the applicant is required to provide the same information, make the same declaration and provide the same authority and other information as for a written application (read the ‘Written application to be the registered contact’ section of this guide). The applicant’s signature is not required.

On receipt of the application, the provider must make a written declaration on behalf of the applicant and notify the applicant of its contents. Notification can be done in several ways:

the declaration can be read back to the applicant over the phone, or in face-to-face contact

a copy of the declaration can be sent back via email or the internet

a copy of the declaration can be faxed or sent by post

The following telephone check list can be downloaded to help you.

Applications to be the registered contact can be scanned and stored digitally in the same way as applications to open the CTF.

CTF providers can accept an application to be the registered contact over the telephone. There is a downloadable document with a set of questions for phone applicants (ODT, 6.93KB).

Change of registered contact

A person cannot take over as the registered contact for a CTF account without the existing registered contact confirming that they agree not to be the registered contact. Without that confirmation the registered contact cannot be changed. The confirmation does not need to be in writing.

The agreement of the existing registered contact is not needed, and should not be requested, in the following cases:

on the death or incapacity of the registered contact

where the registered contact cannot be contacted

where the existing contact is shown as Mrs CTF Liaison Officer (read the section on ‘Revenue allocated accounts’) and the new registered contact is a person with parental responsibility

where a court order which placed a person as a responsible person for the child has expired

where a court has given a Special Guardianship Order

where a court orders that the person who is the registered contact must stop

where the new registered contact has been appointed to be a guardian or special guardian of the child

where the new registered contact has adopted the child under an adoption order (but refer to the section covering where the Share Foundation is the existing registered contact)

where The Share Foundation becomes the registered contact

where the child has reached the age of 16 and has indicated they want to take on the registered contact role

In the case of:

death

incapacity

adoption (where the registered contact applicant claims to have adopted the child)

replacement of the current registered contact by court order

Providers should satisfy themselves that this is so, either by sight of suitable documentation, or from other evidence they hold.

A CTF account cannot be operated under a power of attorney or court order for the registered contact, unless the child is the registered contact. The power of attorney and court order is given by or on behalf of the donor (in this case the registered contact) and it allows the attorney to take decisions about the donor’s own property. The CTF account is not the donor’s property, so where the registered contact lacks the capacity to make decisions about the CTF account, the registered contact needs to be replaced.

Where the registered contact cannot be contacted, for practical purposes a provider can assume that contact has been lost with a registered contact when they have not received any communication from the registered contact within the previous 12 months, and an item of post has been returned undelivered.

If a provider is contacted by a person wishing to become the registered contact for a CTF, and that person asks the provider for details of the existing registered contact, the provider should consider whether they should release this information under their data protection obligations.

If The Share Foundation is the registered contact for a CTF and another person asks to become the registered contact the provider should tell them that The Share Foundation is the registered contact. They should advise the person that there is already somebody assigned as registered contact.

The registered contact cannot be changed without permission from The Share Foundation. CTF providers should tell The Share Foundation that somebody is trying to apply to be the registered contact.

Where an adoptive parent tells the provider that they want to become the registered contact, the provider must not give any details about the existing registered contact or seek the agreement of the existing registered contact to the change. Once the provider has verified the adoptive parent, the provider must update the details held on their systems immediately to make sure that in these very sensitive cases any correspondence only goes to the correct contact. To find out more, read the section on if The Share Foundation is the existing registered contact.

The role of The Share Foundation

Local authorities will inform the Share Foundation when they are looking after a child with a CTF that does not have anyone (or anyone appropriate) with parental responsibility for the child.

The Share Foundation will assume management of the accounts, either until someone with parental responsibility becomes available or until the child reaches the age of 16 and wishes to manage their own account. The Share Foundation will make the declaration and authorisation to the provider required by regulations.

Subscriptions to a CTF

Who can subscribe to a CTF

Any person can subscribe to a CTF by making a payment of money. Transfers of shares or other investments into the CTF is not allowed. The person subscribing does not need to be resident in the UK, nor do they have to be related to the child in any way. Subscriptions to the CTF can be made even if the child is not in the UK.

It must be made clear a subscription made to a CTF is a gift to the child and cannot be repaid if subscriber changes their mind or the payment was made in error. CTF providers can explain this on deposit slips, account information leaflets, their web site, banking applications or verbally for a telephone subscription.

The CTF regulations do not require that the subscriber give a formal signed agreement. To avoid errors providers are advised to make sure that subscribers provide the child’s unique reference number as well as the child’s name.

When a subscription is made to a CTF without contacting the CTF provider, for example, by a bank transfer it can be accepted and the CTF provider does not have to explain to the subscriber that they have made a gift to the child.

When can subscriptions to a CTF be accepted

Since 6 April 2020, the annual subscription limit for how much can be subscribed to a CTF in any subscription year is £9,000 (previously £4,368 from 6 April 2019). Any part of the limit which is not used is lost — it cannot be carried forward or back to other subscription years. Providers must make sure that subscriptions in any subscription year do not exceed the limits. Government contributions do not count toward the subscription limit, nor does any interest, dividends or other income arising from the investments held in the CTF.

The child, the child’s parents or other relatives, local authorities, charities or any other person can subscribe to the CTF. All subscriptions must be made in cash, which may include payment by cheque, Direct Debit, charge card, credit card, direct credit and standing order. CTF rules do not require providers to identify or record the identity of the third party contributor. The registered contact cannot prevent any subscription to the CTF.

The Welsh Government made payments to the CTFs of Welsh children, but these payments ceased at the end of January 2011.

Subscriptions by cheque are valid pending clearance of the cheque. If the cheque is not honoured then no subscription has been made and the figure on the cheque will not count toward the subscription limit. Any subscriptions returned to a subscriber under the Direct Debit Indemnity Scheme are treated in the same way.

The CTF regulations allow subscriptions by lump sum, or by regular or irregular periodic payment, provided the subscription limits are not exceeded. The provider may impose conditions, such as a minimum lump sum subscription, except for stakeholder CTFs, where the provider must accept single subscriptions of £10 or more.

The date of subscription may be important where 2 or more parties wish to subscribe to the CTF, and one of the subscriptions is greater than the amount of unused subscription limit. This is how to determine which subscription is the earliest:

For cheques, use the date that the cheque is received and accepted by the provider (but cheques that are not honoured do not count towards the subscription limit)

For Direct Debits, either the date that the provider applies to draw on the Direct Debit, provided that the cash transfer takes place in due course, or the date that the provider is authorised to draw on the Direct Debit, provided that the cash transfer takes place in due course (if that date is earlier than the date the Direct Debit is received and accepted, then the date of subscription is the later date). A provider can use either method but must do so consistently and apply it to all Direct Debits.

If the subscription is made by debit card, charge card or credit card, use the date the authorisation is given by the subscriber. If it is by direct credit and standing order, use the date that the subscribed funds are received by the provider.

Once a subscription is made to a CTF, the cash (and any investments bought with the cash) are beneficially owned by the child. The subscriber cannot recover their subscription, nor can they (unless they are the registered contact) give any instruction as to how the cash is to be managed or used in the CTF.

The direct transfer of shares or other investments other than cash into a CTF is not allowed. Investments held by a person outside a CTF can be sold, and the proceeds subscribed to the CTF. The sale of the investments is a disposal for capital gains purposes.

Subscription year

The subscription year normally runs from the child’s previous birthday to the day before their next birthday. When a CTF is opened, the subscription year starts on the date it is opened and ends on the day before the child’s next birthday. For a child born on the 29 February, the subscription year runs to the 28 February for all years.

Feeder accounts

Since 6 April 2020 the annual subscription limit is £9,000 in any subscription year. Amounts higher than that cannot go into the CTF until the start of the next subscription year. Providers can set up feeder accounts for excess subscriptions but they are not required to do so under the CTF rules.

The feeder account is not a CTF, and will be treated in the same way as any other children’s savings account for tax purposes.

Direct Debit Indemnity Scheme

Under this scheme, where money is taken out of an account by Direct Debit by mistake, the account holder can claim it back. The account holder’s bank repays the money to the account holder, and claims back that amount from the recipient. Subscribers to a CTF might make a claim under the Direct Debit Indemnity Scheme.

In cases where the subscriptions are reclaimed under the Direct Debit indemnity scheme the subscription will be treated as not made (in the same way as for a failed cheque). If any tax relief on interest has been claimed from HMRC in respect of the unwound subscription it must be repaid to HMRC, and any interest arising may be subject to deduction of tax. A subscription made by Direct Debit may not be unwound unless a successful claim is made under the indemnity scheme.

Generating a cash subscription by disposing of existing investments

Investments held by an individual outside a CTF can be sold, and the proceeds subscribed to a CTF. Subscribers and providers should note that the sale of investments is a disposal for capital gains purposes.

The CTF subscription can be used to buy back often the same investments (but not necessarily so) within the CTF provided certain conditions are met. This is a share exchange (sometimes called ‘Bed and CTFing’) which can apply to units as well as shares.

The conditions that must be met are that:

a) the investments must not be purchased from the investor’s spouse, civil partner or from the investor

b) the investments must be bought at the open market price

c) any Stamp Duty or Stamp Duty Reserve Tax paid on the purchase of CTF investments must be paid out of cash held in the CTF

d) the funds generated by the disposal of the investor’s shares must be available to meet the purchase on settlement day

The subscription date can be the date on which the investor’s shares or units are sold, the settlement date for the purchase, or any date in between that the investor chooses, provided condition (d) is met.

An existing insurance policy cannot be directly transferred into a CTF. However, an existing policy can be surrendered, and the proceeds used to subscribe to a CTF. The surrender would be a chargeable event and may give rise to a capital gain, unless it is a ‘time served’ qualifying policy. A subscription could also be made from the proceeds of a part surrender. Part surrenders may also be chargeable events.

Building society bonus payment

Building societies can pay bonuses to their members in respect of the products they hold and this can include children who hold a CTF account. Bonuses paid in respect of CTF accounts are exempt from tax and do not count towards the annual CTF subscription limit if they are paid directly into the CTF account.

The definition of building society bonus for CTF purposes specifically excludes any bonus arising from demutualisation, merger or sale of a building society subsidiary.

Qualifying investments for the CTF

Qualifying investments in the CTF

The investments that providers may purchase, make or hold in a CTF are:

qualifying shares

qualifying securities

gilt edged securities

strips of gilt-edged securities or any securities issued on or behalf of a government of any EEA state

shares in qualifying investment trusts

units or shares in a UK Undertakings for Collective Investment in Transferable Securities (UCITS) or a recognised UCITS

fractional interests

depositary interests

cash deposits

units or shares in non-UCITS retail schemes

alternative finance arrangements

policies of life insurance

certain core capital deferred shares

securities, other than National Savings certificates, Premium Savings Bonds, National Savings Stamps and National gift tokens, issued under the National Loans Act 1968 or the National Savings Bank Act 1971, on terms which provide for them to be held in the CTF

Any fund recognised under the Temporary Marketing Permissions Regime (TMPR) on 1 October 2024 will continue to be treated as a recognised fund. This is until the end of the transition period on 31 December 2026 and includes new funds created under an umbrella fund.

From 1 January 2027, only recognised Overseas Funds Regime (OFR) funds will qualify for inclusion.

All other kinds of investments are not qualifying investments and may not be held in a CTF.

Certain qualifying investments may not be held in a stakeholder CTF — for further details of these read the section on ‘Restrictions on qualifying investments held in a stakeholder CTF’.

Qualifying shares

Qualifying shares are shares, not being shares in an investment trust, issued by a company which is incorporated anywhere in the world, and which are either:

officially listed on a recognised stock exchange, including Co-operative Societies and Community Benefit Societies (Industrial and Provident Societies in Northern Ireland)

admitted to trading on a recognised stock exchange in the EEA (shares admitted to trading on EEA markets included in Tables 1 and 2 published on GOV.UK can qualify for the CTF if they satisfy the other requirements in this paragraph)

Qualifying shares do not include, for example:

shares in unquoted companies

shares traded on Ofex

nil paid rights (purchased in the market by the provider)

warrants to subscribe for shares (read the ‘Warrants’ section of this guide)

Fractional interests

For the purposes of the CTF regulations, a ‘fractional interest’ is a contractual arrangement between you (the CTF provider) and the named child, that allows them to invest in a proportion of a whole share that is held by you or your nominee.

Fractional interests of a whole share are eligible to be held in a CTF if they meet the following criteria:

the fractional interest is held by an approved CTF provider

the relevant whole share, including shares in an investment trust and shares in a fund, must be a qualifying investment for the purposes of the CTF regulations

the relevant whole share is either:

officially listed on a recognised stock exchange

admitted to trading on a recognised stock exchange in the UK or the EEA

the whole share is held in your name or the name of your nominee — you cannot delegate below the level of nominee

the fractional interest contractual arrangement is between you and the named child and set out within the terms and conditions of the account

the named child has beneficial ownership of the fractional interest

transactions in fractional interests meet the requirements of the general investment rules — the price of the fractional interest is the proportion of the price of the whole share, which is the price that might be reasonably expected if traded on the open market

transfers or withdrawals of fractional interests are actioned within 30 days

For fractional interests, the general conditions regarding general meetings and voting rights do not apply.

If a named child holds multiple fractional interests amounting to a relevant whole share, then the investor rights relating to a whole share will apply.

If there are changes to the whole share, you should follow the guidance given for changes to investments held in the CTF.

Qualifying securities

Qualifying securities are securities which have been issued by a company, which is incorporated anywhere in the world, and which satisfy at least one of the following 3 conditions.

Securities in an investment trust are qualifying investments provided the securities meet at least one of the following 3 conditions and the trust has no eligible rental income (defined in section 508A of the Income and Corporation Taxes Act 1988).

The 3 conditions of which at least one must be satisfied are that the securities, the shares in the company issuing the securities, or the company issuing the securities is a 75% subsidiary of a company whose shares are listed or admitted to trading on the official list of a recognised stock exchange.

Shares in investment trusts

Shares in an investment trust listed or admitted to trading on the official list of a registered Stock Exchange are qualifying investments for the CTF. This includes shares with warrants attached purchased by the provider in the course of a public offer.

Where providers apply for shares in an investment trust using cash within a CTF they may retain in the CTF any warrants attached to the shares acquired in the course of the public offer. Any warrants received subsequently are not qualifying investments and must be sold. New issues of warrants offered to existing shareholders only cannot be taken up or held in the CTF.

Depository interests

UK regulation requires securities to be electronically settled (in CREST). For companies registered outside the UK, this is achieved through a depositary interest (DI) mechanism. The DI is effectively an electronic ‘wrapper’ around the ordinary share, to facilitate securities to be held electronically rather than in paper form. A company applies for DIs representing ordinary shares to be admitted to CREST with effect from its admission to the market.

When checking the details of international shares officially listed on the Registered Stock Exchange (RSE) or admitted to trading on the Alternative Investment Market (AIM), the descriptor of each security will identify the listed or traded instrument (for example ordinary shares).

Reference to DI in the descriptor simply confirms that the shares are settled electronically through CREST, and therefore is not relevant in determining CTF eligibility (because it is the shares that are listed or admitted to trading, not the DI).

Depositary receipts

A depositary receipts (DR) is a type of security and should not be confused with depository interests. A DR can be held in an Individual Savings Account (ISA) providing the underlying shares represented by the DR are in the beneficial ownership of the holder and are themselves ISA qualifying. It is irrelevant for CTF purposes whether the DR is listed or traded on a RSE.

Where the listed or traded instrument is a depository receipt, for example a global depository receipt (GDR), the descriptor will clearly state this. This can be checked on the UKLA Official List for listed investments.

American depositary receipt and American depositary share

An American depositary share (ADS) is a vehicle for foreign corporations to list their ordinary equity on an American stock exchange. Foreign corporations are not permitted to make direct secondary listings on American stock exchanges, so this form of indirect ownership has been devised. ADSs enable US investors to buy the securities of a foreign company without the accompanying risks or inconveniences of cross-border and cross-currency transactions.

ADSs are dollar denominated and each share represents one or more underlying shares in the foreign corporation. An American depositary receipt (ADR) is a physical certificate evidencing ownership in one or several ADSs. The terms ADR and ADS are often used interchangeably.

The decision of the first tier tribunal in the Stamp Duty Reserve Tax case of HSBC Holdings and Bank of New York Mellon v Commissioners for HMRC, UKFTT 163 (TC) has shown that in some cases where an ADR is involved, beneficial ownership may not rest with the underlying investor.

Where a DR is issued in the UK, HMRC’s view is that the holder of a DR is the beneficial owner of the underlying investments, so the DR can be a qualifying investment.

Where a DR is issued outside the UK the question of whether the holder of the DR is the beneficial owner of the underlying investments will be determined by reference to the law of the territory in which the DR is issued. Information on beneficial ownership may be provided to investors by the depository.

Where the relevant law means that the holder of a DR is not the beneficial owner of the underlying investments, the DR cannot be a qualifying investment that can be held in a stocks and shares ISA.

Where beneficial ownership of the underlying investments cannot conclusively be determined by reference to the law governing the arrangements relating to the issue of the DRs, for tax purposes HMRC will continue to determine beneficial ownership according to its understanding of the principles of UK law. This means that HMRC will continue to apply its long-standing practice of regarding the holder of a DR as holding the beneficial interest in the underlying investments.

CTF providers should therefore check the terms and conditions and any other documentation related to the DR for any reference to the beneficial ownership of the underlying investments. In the absence of any conclusive information to show that the holder of the DR is not the beneficial owner of the underlying investments, the CTF provider can assume that the holder of a DR is the beneficial owner, so the DR can be a qualifying investment.

Where the holder of the DR is the beneficial owner of the underlying investments, a practical test that managers can apply to determine whether the DR is a qualifying investment is to look through the DR to the underlying investments represented by the DR. This might require looking through intermediaries. If all the underlying investments (other than cash) would be qualifying investments for the CTF if held directly by the investor, the DR will be a qualifying investment.

If the investor holds an ADS or ADR that is traded on a US stock exchange, the underlying investment is the shares represented by the ADS or ADR. If these shares are officially listed on a recognised stock exchange, the ADS or ADR will be a qualifying investment for stocks and shares CTF.

In some cases the investor cannot hold shares directly (for example, when the shares are issued in the form of a global note). The test should then be applied as if the investor were capable of holding the shares.

The CTF regulations list investments that can be held in a CTF. They do not list those that cannot be held. In the same way, we cannot produce a complete list of DIs that do not qualify. Here is a list of a few of the DIs that would not qualify:

DIs representing short-term loan notes

DIs representing cash

DIs representing a basket of investments where any of the investments would not qualify for a CTF

Cash

Any cash subscribed to or held in a CTF must be in sterling and must be deposited in an account with a deposit-taker, a deposit account or a share account with a building society, which is designated as a CTF.

The CTF-designated account may also include other savings products, such as feeder funds and current account balances provided the account is designated as a CTF account and the monies relating to each product are recorded and can be accounted for separately. The same account may also be designated in other ways, for example if the account also holds ISA cash, the account may be named the CTF and ISA Client Money Account.

Where a person wishes to subscribe currency other than sterling to a CTF where the cash is held in sterling, the amount subscribed must be converted to sterling before it can be subscribed to the CTF.

Units or shares in non-UCITS retail schemes

Non-UCITS retail schemes are defined in the COLL. In order for the shares or units in a non-UCITS retail scheme to qualify for the CTF the instrument constituting the scheme must provide for redemption of the units or shares no less frequently than bimonthly.

Alternative finance arrangements

Savings under alternative finance arrangements falling within section 47 or 49 of the Finance Act 2005, for example Sharia accounts, qualify for the CTF.

Policies of life insurance

A policy of life insurance (as determined under general law) is a qualifying investment for a CTF if:

the policy is on the life of the child only (joint life, multiple life and life of another policies are not allowed)

the terms and conditions of the policy provide that:

the policy may only be owned or held as a qualifying investment for a CTF

the policy shall terminate automatically if it comes to the notice of the provider that that it fails to meet the requirement that it falls within section I or 3 of Part 2 of Schedule 1 to Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 if it includes subsidiary benefits such as a sickness, critical illness, accident or waiver of premium benefit

the proceeds from the termination of the policy, or the partial surrender of the rights conferred by the policy cannot be paid to the child whilst the policy is held in the CTF

the policy, the rights conferred by the policy and any share or interest in the policy or rights respectively, are not capable of assignment or assignation, other than that the policy may be transferred within the CTF from one provider to another (read the ‘External transfer’ section of this guide) and the rights may vest in the personal representatives of a deceased child

the policy evidences or secures a contract of insurance which either falls within section I or 3 of part 2 of schedule 1 to the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001, or would fall within either of those sections if the insurer was a company with permission under part 4 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 to effect or carry out contracts of insurance (for example, if the body is an EU insurer providing insurance on a services basis and subject to home state authorisation in accordance with article 6 of the First Council Directive 79/267/EEC)

the policy is not:

a contract to pay an annuity on human life

a personal portfolio bond within the meaning of section 516 of the Income Tax (Trading and Other Income) Act 2005

a contract, the effecting and carrying out of which constitutes ‘pension business’ within the meaning of section 431B(1) of the Income and Corporation Taxes Act 1988

after the first payment in respect of a premium in relation to the policy has been made, there is no contractual obligation on any person to make any other such payment

no sum may be lent to the child, or the registered contact, or at their direction, by arrangement with the insurer with whom the policy is held

Where the account provider is an insurance company or a friendly society and the investments in the CTF include a life insurance policy the title to that policy, and the policy documentation evidencing the title, must be held by the registered contact (read the section on the ‘Registered contact’).

Where CTF subscriptions are applied as premiums under a CTF policy, and the subscriptions are payable in instalments, there must be no obligation to pay any instalment (or any premium) other than the first one. But this does not prevent subscriptions being made by Direct Debit or standing order arrangements. Regular premium policies including ‘qualifying policies’ (schedule 15 of the Income and Corporation Taxes Act 1988 defines a ‘qualifying policy’) are not permissible investments.

A policy may satisfy the requirement that it falls within section I or 3 of part 2 of schedule 1 to the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 if it includes subsidiary benefits such as a sickness, critical illness, accident or waiver of premium benefit.

If there has been a breach of any of the conditions in the section on ‘Policies of life insurance’, and the breach cannot be repaired, or has not been remedied in a reasonable time, then the policy shall automatically terminate.

For more information, read the ‘Repairing CTFs’ section of this guide.

Restrictions on qualifying investments held in a stakeholder CTF

Certain types of investment may not be held directly in a stakeholder CTF, although they may be held indirectly through a qualifying relevant collective investment scheme, such as a UK UCITS or a recognised UCITS.

The investments that cannot be held directly in a stakeholder CTF are:

shares in an investment trust

securities of an investment trust

rights in with-profits endowment policies

rights under a contract of insurance in a with-profits fund

units or shares in a relevant collective investment scheme unless it is a requirement of that scheme that the purchase and sale price of those units shall, at any given time, not differ from each other and that the price must be made available to the public on a daily basis

rights under a contract of insurance which are expressed as shares in funds held by the insurer unless it is a requirement of the contract of insurance that the purchase and sale price of those shares shall, at any given time, not differ from each other and that the price must be made available to the public on a daily basis

shares issued by a company wherever incorporated and officially listed on a recognised stock exchange

securities issued by a company and securities under the National Loans Act 1968, unless the contract entered into for purchase of the securities or gilt strips (or any other contract) has the effect that the value of the securities or gilt strips cannot at any time fall below 80% of the consideration paid for the securities or gilt strips whilst they are being held in the CTF

cash held in deposit accounts, or in a building society share account, unless the interest payable on a daily basis is paid at a rate not less than 1% below the Bank of England base rate (where the base rate increases the interest rate for the deposit account must satisfy this condition within one month of the date of increase)

depositary interests, where the investments concerned are investments of any of the kinds listed in the previous points

cryptoasset Exchange Traded Notes (cETNs)

Shares being brought to listing

Providers may apply for shares being brought to listing on behalf of a child using cash from within a CTF provided:

they will be qualifying shares (read the section on ‘Qualifying shares’) or shares in a qualifying investment trust within 30 calendar days of the date on which the shares are allotted or allocated

they were not allocated in connection with the allocation of other shares, securities or units

Providers can use cash held in a CTF to apply for public offer shares brought to the market by an offer for sale, or an offer for subscription. Providers cannot use cash held in a CTF to purchase shares brought to the market by an intermediaries’ offer, or a placing.

Shares paid for in instalments

Providers must meet any instalment due in respect of the shares held in the CTF from funds within the CTF. The instalment payments may not be funded from cash held outside the CTF. If sufficient funds are not held in the CTF, investments held within the CTF may be sold to meet the instalment.

Changes to investments held in the CTF

The most common examples of a change to an investment are:

takeovers

demergers

capital reorganisations (other than a rights issue or bonus issue)

rights issues

bonus issues

Providers may take up any offer to shareholders in respect of investments held in the CTF. Whether the resulting shares can be held in the CTF will depend on whether they are qualifying investments. Where the new investments are qualifying investments, they can remain in the CTF. Where they are not qualifying investments, providers must sell them within 30 calendar days of the date they became non-qualifying investments and the proceeds must remain in the CTF. If the non-qualifying investments are not sold within the 30 days, the CTF must be repaired (read the section on ‘Repairing CTFs’).

Complex reorganisations often involve more than just the issue of one set of new investments. There could, for example, be a bonus issue of shares, which are replaced in turn by other shares, which are then sold, or converted to other investments. If the intermediate investments are not eligible for a CTF then, strictly, the final investments, or cash proceeds, cannot be held in the CTF even if the final investments themselves are eligible.

However, where ineligible investments are issued as an intermediate stage, and those investments are short-lived, or are automatically replaced by cash, CTF Support will consider whether it is possible to look through the intermediate stages and apply the qualifying investments guidance to the initial and final investments alone. If a reorganisation involves intermediate ineligible investments providers should submit full details to CTF Support and, if possible, well before the planned reorganisation date.

Rights issues and other offers to shareholders

Providers may use only cash within the CTF to take up rights issues and other offers for qualifying investments. Providers must reinvest in the CTF any proceeds received from lapsed rights. The proceeds do not count as a subscription.

Bonus issues

Providers must add to a CTF bonus issues of shares or units received in respect of an investment held in the CTF, provided the shares or units in the bonus issue are qualifying investments. Such bonus issues do not count towards the CTF subscription limit. Where they are non-qualifying investments, providers should follow the qualifying investments guidance.

Connected accounts

A deposit account, or share account with a building society, in a CTF must not be connected to any investment held by the child or any other person other than an ISA, Junior ISA or a CTF.

A CTF is connected with another investment if it was:

opened or acquired with reference to the other investment

opened or acquired with a view to enabling the other investment to be opened on particular terms, or facilitating the opening of the other investment on particular terms (and the terms on which the CTF was opened would have been significantly less favourable if the other investment had not been opened or acquired)

HMRC will accept that a deposit or share account is not connected to a CTF if it is a feeder account opened to enable subscribers to fund future deposits into the CTF, provided that the interest on the feeder account is in line with the interest paid on the provider’s other savings accounts.

Cryptoasset Exchange Traded Notes (cETNs)

UK cryptoasset ETNs cannot be held as qualifying investments in a Child Trust Fund.

Any cETNs already held within a Child Trust Fund immediately before 6 April 2026 will continue to be treated as qualifying investments for as long as they remain held in that account.

No new subscriptions, purchases or switching of cETNs are permitted into a Child Trust Fund from 6 April 2026.

You must ensure systems prevent new acquisitions of cETNs into a Child Trust Fund.

Is the investment a qualifying security

To find out if the investment is a qualifying security, answer the following questions:

Is the investment a security?

If the answer is no, the investment is not a qualifying security.

If the answer is yes, move on to the next question:

Is the security is issued by a company?

If the answer is no, the investment is not a qualifying security.

If the answer is yes, move on to the next question:

Is the company issuing the security a 75% subsidiary of a company whose shares are listed or admitted to trading on the official list of a recognised stock exchange?

If the answer is yes, the investment is a qualifying security.

If the answer is no, move on to the next question:

Are the shares in the company issuing the security listed or admitted to trading on the official list of a recognised stock exchange?

If the answer is yes, the investment is a qualifying security.

If the answer is no, move on to the next question:

Are the securities listed or admitted to trading on the official list of a recognised stock exchange?

If the answer is yes, the investment is a qualifying security.

If the answer is no, the investment is not a qualifying security.

Management of the CTF

Delegation of the provider’s functions
